newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Masked men discuss crime with South African ministers.
newsitem.headline: Masked men discuss crime with South African ministers.

text.p: South African cabinet ministers held crime prevention talks on Tuesday with Moslem vigilantes, three of whom were reported to have sat through the meeting with Palestinian-style scarves wrapped around their faces.

Justice Minister Dullah Omar, who attended with prisons minister Sipho Mzimela and police minister Sydney Mufamadi, told a news conference the closed talks had focused on whether members of the PAGAD vigilante group should be allowed to march in public with guns and masks.
PAGAD (People Against Gangsterism and Drugs) sprung into prominence in August when members torched and killed the leader of a Cape Town drugs gang after marching through his neighbourhood.

A month ago a PAGAD member was shot dead during clashes with police who were trying to disperse a demonstration by the vigilantes at Cape Town's tourist-thronged waterfront shopping and entertainment mall.

Omar, seated next to three PAGAD men with scarves around their heads and faces, told the news conference the meeting on Tuesday agreed to set up a committee to try to rule whether PAGAD should be allowed to parade with guns and masks.
Asked if he regarded it as normal to address a news conference on the same platform as masked men, Omar said:
"Some people wear headgear, others don't. I do not divert the importance of the meeting by paying attention to issues like those."
A participant in the meeting told reporters the three had also worn their masks during the talks, but Omar declined to confirm this. "I didn't notice. There were so many people there."
The three refused to give their names at the news conference.
A non-masked PAGAD member, Achmat Cassiem, said PAGAD members wore masks to prevent crime. If gangsters could not recognise them, they could not attack them, he said.
Cassiem said PAGAD members carried guns only for self-defence. He denied reports that the movement wanted to install an Islamic fundamentalist government in South Africa.
PAGAD members accuse police of not doing enough to keep their communities safe from drugs dealers and other criminals.
